entries.title: The Pit: why a 50% loss needs +100%
entries.hook: Lose half. Now you must double just to break even.
entries.takeaway: A loss is measured from where you started, but the climb back is measured from what is left. So the climb is always the bigger percentage, and it grows faster the deeper the pit.

entries.title: 35% winners can beat 60% winners
entries.hook: 60% winners vs 35% winners. Guess who's losing.
entries.takeaway: How often you win is only half the math. A 60% win rate with small wins and big losses loses money; a 35% win rate with small losses and big wins makes it. The price of the second one is long losing streaks, so plan for them.
entries.question: Can a 35% win rate beat a 60% win rate?

entries.title: R: the only unit a trader needs
entries.hook: You made $500. Proud? Depends what you risked.
entries.takeaway: R is what you lose if your stop gets hit: (entry − stop) × shares, fixed before you buy. Measure every result with that ruler. A $500 win is +5R on $100 risk and +0.25R on $2,000. Losers should all be −1R; anything bigger means the stop moved or price gapped.

entries.title: Legend 01: Jesse Livermore
entries.hook: Made $1 million in a day. Went bankrupt more than once.
entries.takeaway: Jesse Livermore taught himself to read markets from prices, won big in the 1907 panic and the 1929 crash, and built his method around the pivotal point: wait for a key price to break, add only while the trade works, then sit tight. He lost fortunes by breaking those rules: following a friend's cotton tips, buying more as cotton fell, and putting money into businesses outside trading. His 1940 rules are the lessons those losses paid for.

entries.title: The Seesaw: wider stop, smaller size
entries.hook: Always buy 100 shares? Nice round number.
entries.takeaway: Fix the risk first (say 1% of the account), then let the stop set the size: shares = risk ÷ stop distance, rounded down. A wider stop means fewer shares and the same dollars at risk. Buying the same share count every time lets your stop decide your risk instead.
